timeline.text: design chosen (two-wheel plus caster for carpet and hard floor, LiFePO4 battery). Parametric hub and coupon modelled in CadQuery; servo.toml holds placeholders until measured.

scope widened to a household robot (recognition, per-person behaviour, memory, household rules) with a v2 arm for tidying toys. Privacy rules handed to the owner (ADR 0013, superseding 0007 and 0012); folder renamed from exp003-home-robot.

horn measured on a spare STS3215 (19.9 mm aluminium horn, 4 M3 holes on 13.6 mm, centre screw 2 mm proud). Hub web thickened so the centre pocket stays below the screw counterbores. Coupon ready to print.

the lab's screw kit is button head with M3 only from 8 mm, so the model now takes the screws on hand ([screws] in servo.toml) and thickens the web (7.95 mm) until an M3 x 8 stops 0.5 mm short of the servo case. Fixed with 4 x M3 x 8 button head.

H2D set up (firmware 01.04.20.00, AMS 2 Pro on the right nozzle). First print: the hub coupon in PETG Basic, servo side down, 0.2 mm layers, 4 walls, 30% infill, no supports, textured PEI plate (22 min, 8.3 g). Snug fit on the horn with 4 x M3 x 8 button head and the default 0.2 mm clearance; screws pull it flat and it spins free. But it cleared the servo by only about two sheets of paper (design: 2.5 mm): the case is low round the shaft, and a raised block under the label starts right at the horn's edge, 2.0 mm below the horn top (new measurement I, raised_case_mm). A 1.5 mm recess wrapping round the horn left 0.5 mm over it.

hub redesigned to sit flat on the horn's top face, centred by the centre pocket (5.4 mm over the 5.0 mm screw head) and the screws. It now clears the case by 2.0 mm, the new minimum (it was 1.0); the model steps the underside up beyond the horn if a case needs more. Web 6.45 mm, still 4 x M3 x 8. Reprint the coupon to confirm before the full hub.
coupon v2 (flat seat) printed in PETG (20 min, 7.2 g) and fits well on the horn. Kept as the fit gauge and phase 0 spin indicator. Next: two full wheel hubs.

both full wheel hubs printed together in PETG, servo side down, no supports (2 h 44 min, 118.5 g). Clean prints; each seats on the horn like the coupon and spins true without touching the case. Next: the TPU tire, once the TPU arrives.

STS3215 CAD model vendored from The Robot Studio's SO-ARM100 repo (Apache-2.0) in cad/vendor/. A caliper on a spare confirmed the case (45.4 x 24.8 mm) and the top mounting holes (20.7 x 20.4 mm centre to centre) exactly; the horn differs by 0.3 to 0.5 mm, so the hub keeps its measured numbers. The idler disc on the bottom stands about 4.1 mm proud of the case bottom round the shaft, so anything under the servo needs a pocket. Case numbers in servo.toml [case], checked by the tests.

TPU tire modelled (cad/exp003_cad/tire.py): a 120 mm ring with a 107 mm bore that grips the 108 mm rim seat (0.9% stretch) and a lip over each flange, 0.2 mm clear, so it cannot walk off sideways. Fitting it means stretching 3.7% over one flange. Tests check the only contact with the hub is the grip band on the seat. Prints flat in TPU 95A, no supports.
printed rim measured across the top flange (110.6 mm, design 111.0), so the seat is about 107.6 mm. The tire's bore is now sized to it (106.6 mm, [tire] in servo.toml).

full survey of the STS3215 model after a bracket was pitched for the top holes without checking the rest of the case. The bottom has its own four holes (24.5 x 20.5 mm, confirmed present), the two bus connectors, a step and a raised pad. All recorded in cad/vendor/README.md and servo.toml; a "Before designing a part" checklist now gates every printed part (cad/README, pointed to from AGENTS.md).

servo cradle modelled (cad/exp003_cad/cradle.py), following the new checklist. It holds the servo by its bottom holes because the top holes sit only about 2.5 mm under the spinning hub. It is a U: the back wall has four 0.5 mm pads and one opening for the idler disc, connectors and pad; cheeks hug the case 0.2 mm clear; the lower cheek is the foot, with M3 ears. The supplied M2 x 6 screws go 3.5 mm into the case. Tests load the vendored servo model into the cradle and find no clashes; the clash check fails as it should on a servo lowered 0.6 mm. The wheel axle sits 15.6 mm above the foot, which the base plate will need.

servo cradle sent to print in PETG (34 min, 10.0 g). Base plate inputs gathered with sources in cad/BASE_PLATE.md; the caster's mounting height is not published anywhere and is measured on arrival. Owner chose the widest stance: battery across between the servos, 330 mm over the tires, a 300 x 262 mm one-piece plate. Balance check: centre of mass 46 mm behind the axle, 18 mm with a 1 kg v2 arm at full forward reach.

the first servo cradle is printed and fitted. The servo slides in well, sits flat on the pads and holds solid with the supplied M2 x 6 screws. The loose metal idler disc on the servo's bottom comes off first (only a two-sided bracket holds it) and goes with the spares. The second cradle printed and fitted perfectly too: both wheel servos are in their cradles.

most of the 2026-11-17 order arrived (Pi 5, XT60s, fuses and limit switches due 2026-11-21). The two TPU tires are printing on the right hotend: TPU 95A goes through the rear TPU inlet once the right hotend's tube is moved there from the AMS buffer (Bambu's H2 TPU guide). Generic TPU profile, 3 walls, 25% gyroid, 8 h 8 min, 105 g.

both tires printed cleanly and fit the hubs snugly on the first try, with the bore sized to the caliper reading of the printed rim (107.6 mm seat, 1.0 mm interference). Both wheels are complete. No reprint needed. The printer is now laid out with the AMS on the left nozzle and the right nozzle kept for TPU (docs/printing.md), so the bumper prints with no tube swap.

caster measured (50 mm to the top of its plate, holes on 36 x 28 mm centres). That settles the base plate's height: the cradles sit on top of the plate, whose top face is 44.4 mm off the floor, and the caster bolts into a raised pocket (cad/BASE_PLATE.md, "Height"). The bumper waits until the plate is modelled.

the caster's raised pocket is a separate light cup (cad/exp003_cad/caster_cup.py), so the base plate can print flat. The cup is printing as the fit test: the caster's plate must drop in and the fork must swivel clear of its walls.

first cup fitted. The caster's plate drops in (slight play) and the holes line up, but the fork hits the walls when it swivels. Its sweep was never measured; it reaches 24 mm from the swivel axis. Cup v2 adds a 25.5 mm radius circle to the cavity.

cup v2 (light fit-test version) passed: the caster's plate drops in, the holes line up, and the fork swivels clear all the way round. The caster mount is settled; the base plate takes a matching hole.

battery confirmed as an EP1210 from its label. Its F2 spade terminals sit on top at one short end, so the base plate needs only the footprint and straps. 6.3 mm female spade terminals are not on hand: ordered the same day (AIRIC 100-pack, due by 2026-11-25).

base plate modelled. It holds the cradles, the caster cup (now bolted to the plate through four bosses), the battery with fences and strap slots, and hole patterns for the electronics deck, bumper, forward sensors and cliff sensors. Every screw is M3 or M4 with a nut. Checking it against the real cradle model caught a layout error: two identical cradles cannot both point their servos' far ends back, so one points forward. The caster moved to 158 mm behind the axle to keep the cup on the plate.
battery straps measured (21.5 mm wide, 27.5 mm at the buckle); the strap slots are sized to the strap, threaded free end first. The plate is ready to print.
base plate printed (4 h 56 min, 223 g PETG). Next: fit the cradles, the battery and the caster cup (still to print at full strength).

robot console step 1 built on fake wheels (CONTROL_APP.md, ADR 0014): the robot's agent serves a phone app on the home network; hold-to-drive with a 300 ms lease, a watchdog stop, one driver at a time, pairing by link, fake sensor readings marked "no sensor". Each task had a spec and a code review; the reviews found and fixed a dozen ways the wheels could have been left turning (refused, dropped or failed commands, reconnects, a second phone) before any real wheel.

chassis assembled. Both cradles bolted to the plate (4 x M3 x 12 and nuts; the two servos point opposite ways, as identical cradles must), the caster bolted into the full cup (M4 x 12 stood well proud of the nuts, so M4 x 8) and the cup bolted to the plate. On the floor the robot leaned back toward the caster: the cup's cavity had been sized as if the cup started at the plate's underside, but it sits on the top face, so the plate's 4 mm was counted twice and the caster sat 4 mm high. The model is fixed (cup 8.6 mm tall, M3 x 16 to the plate) with a test that the plate, cup and caster heights add up; the corrected cup prints tomorrow. The printer is busy with a toy garbage truck.

corrected caster cup printed (27 min 24 s, 9.89 g PETG) and fitted: the caster into the cup with its 4 x M4 x 8, the cup to the plate with 4 x M3 x 16 and nuts. The robot now sits perfectly level on the floor. The chassis is done.
the Pi 5, XT60 leads and fuse assortment (arrived 2026-11-21) are logged; the limit switches are still to come. The build page and site log are brought up to date.

electronics deck designed (cad/DECK.md) and printed. A fit coupon settled the rocker cutout, the M2.5 standoff boss and the UCTRONICS channel first. Three parts: the compute tray (Pi 5 on 11 mm standoffs, the UCTRONICS behind it), a bridge over the caster cup for the servo board, and the power tray (DROK on slotted pads, INA226, fuse ties, switch and charge-socket panel). The power tray and bridge are printed; the compute tray followed the same evening. The e-stop moved to v2: v1 runs only under the owner's supervision, and the main rocker is its one hardware cut. Soldering and wiring tools ordered; next is a dry fit of all three parts, then the power harness.

in the evening all three deck parts were dry-fitted on the plate. A CAD overlay on the owner's top-view photo matched the layout; the servo board and the INA226 each turn half a turn, and the assembly order is written up in cad/DECK.md. Then the wheels were found "bending". The +y cradle had rolled about the inboard edge of its foot, the servo's outer end lifted and the wheel leaned in. - Cause: each cradle's two bolts sit on one line 11 mm from that edge while the tire pushes 53 mm out (a 4.7 to 1 lever), and the cheeks take the bending across their print layers. - Plan: wheel module v2, with a boxed servo mount on a wide six-bolt foot (printed on its end), an axle beam tying the two sides together, and a base plate v2. Later, a 6806 bearing so the servo only drives. - A ninth checklist rule: trace the load path (cad/WHEEL_MOUNT.md). - The deck waits for plate v2.

wheel module v2 modelled: both servo boxes and the axle beam in one PETG piece, both servos' far ends back, 15 x M3 to a new plate v2. The owner asked for it "hella sturdy", so every check runs at 5 x the static load with the v2 arm reaching forward (73 N a wheel): lever 1.6 to 1 (the cradles were 4.7), 57 N on each outboard bolt, 0.5 MPa in the walls. The wall under the case stays 3 mm so the axle keeps its height. An 18 g coupon checks the servo fit first; the rear brace became a 45-degree-tapered fin after the slicer flagged it as a floating cantilever.

coupon passed; the wheel module printed (164.26 g). No plate v2: the owner asked not to waste filament, and v2 only moved 15 holes, so plate v1 is drilled with the module as its template (1/8 inch bit; cad/WHEEL_MOUNT.md, "Drilling plate v1").

plate v1 drilled (15 holes), both servos into the module (bodies to the rear), wheels on, module bolted to the plate. A crack then showed through the +y box's 5 mm top wall, across a layer joint at mid-span.

the crack stitched with binder-ring wire sunk with the soldering iron (thick office staples would not sink) and a melted bead over it; the owner passed the load check by hand. The electronics deck went on in the DECK.md order: standoffs into the trays, the three parts to the plate, the DROK, INA226 and UCTRONICS, then the Pi 5 with its Active Cooler and the servo board (turned half a turn so its USB-C and power face the Pi). Lessons in BUILD_STEPS.md and cad/DECK.md: the trays' M3 holes are plain (only the bridge legs hold their nuts), zip ties have to be threaded before a tray is bolted down, the DROK sits flush with the plate's right edge. Next: zip ties and screws restock, then the power harness.

wiring plan drafted (HARNESS.md) and checked by building to it: a 3 A fuse added on the charge lead, no e-stop in v1. First soldering session (the owner's first real harness work): the rocker's two leads, each a 16 AWG red wire twisted with one lead of an inline fuse holder (3 A on tab A, 5 A on tab B), tinned, laid flat on the tinned tab and reflowed at 370 C, then heat-shrunk. Beep test passed. Method and lessons in HARNESS.md, "Bench method". Screws and ties restock ordered (due Dec 1 to 5).
